mcqs.question: Why ask whether the risk is a race condition or just a visibility problem before writing any fix?
options: Because visibility problems only occur on single-core machines, so multi-core systems only have races
It changes which fix is appropriate — volatile alone fixes visibility but not a race that needs atomicity
Because Java requires you to name the bug type before compiling synchronized code
Because races can only happen with more than two threads, so the distinction only matters with three or more
mcqs.explanation: Volatile guarantees visibility of a single field but not atomicity of a compound read-modify-write — a true race needs a lock or atomic type. Visibility bugs are a memory-model issue that exists on any modern multi-core CPU regardless of core count, and thread count doesn't gate whether a race is possible.

mcqs.question: In the fixed RequestCounter, why does get() also need to be synchronized, not just increment()?
options: Without synchronizing get(), there's no guarantee the reading thread observes the latest write — the visibility half of the fix
Because get() also performs a read-modify-write that would otherwise race
Because synchronized methods execute faster than unsynchronized ones
Because Java requires every method in a class to use the same set of keywords
mcqs.explanation: get() only reads one field, so it has no read-modify-write race — but without synchronizing on the same monitor, the reading thread has no visibility guarantee into increment()'s writes. Java has no such keyword-uniformity rule, and synchronization doesn't speed up individual calls.

mcqs.question: Under heavy contention, how do the synchronized-lock fix and the AtomicInteger fix typically fail against each other?
options: Both approaches spin indefinitely and never let a thread proceed
The synchronized fix throws an exception on the second thread encountering the lock
AtomicInteger requires a separate lock file to coordinate across threads
The synchronized fix blocks waiting threads; AtomicInteger's CAS loop retries them without blocking, at the cost of wasted retry cycles
mcqs.explanation: Locks block waiting threads until the holder releases; CAS-based atomics never block, they just retry the compare-and-swap, burning CPU on failed attempts instead. Neither throws an exception on contention, and atomics need no external coordination file.

mcqs.question: A class wraps a ConcurrentHashMap and still has a race in `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, compute())`. Why doesn't switching to ConcurrentHashMap alone fix it?
options: ConcurrentHashMap only protects each individual call, not a compound operation spanning the check and the put across two calls
ConcurrentHashMap doesn't support containsKey at all
ConcurrentHashMap is slower than a plain HashMap so the race just happens less often, not never
The race only exists if the map has more than one thread reading from it simultaneously
mcqs.explanation: Each ConcurrentHashMap call is thread-safe in isolation, but containsKey and put here are two separate calls — another thread can insert between them regardless of collection type. ConcurrentHashMap fully supports containsKey, and the fix is a single atomic call like computeIfAbsent, not just a speed difference.
